Clinical Reference

Thyroid Storm & Hyperthyroidism

On this page
Thyrotoxicosis is the clinical state of excess thyroid hormone action; thyroid storm is its life-threatening, decompensated extreme — a hypermetabolic emergency with fever, tachyarrhythmia, and altered mentation carrying ~8–25% mortality even when treated.
Graves = most common cause (~70%) TSH suppressed <0.01, free T4/T3 ↑ Burch-Wartofsky ≥45 → storm Anchor: β-blocker + thionamide + iodine + steroid ATA 2016 · JTA 2016
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

The thyroid follicular cell runs a small factory. It traps iodide from blood through the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), pumps it to the colloid, and thyroid peroxidase (TPO) attaches iodine onto tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin (organification) and couples them into T4 and T3. Hormone is stored on thyroglobulin and released by proteolysis. In blood, the bulk product T4 is a prohormone; peripheral deiodinases (D1/D2) convert it to the ~4× more potent T3, which enters the nucleus and turns up the metabolic thermostat of nearly every tissue.

Thyroid hormone also increases the number and sensitivity of β-adrenergic receptors, so a normal level of circulating catecholamines produces an exaggerated sympathetic effect — tachycardia, tremor, sweating, brisk reflexes. This is why β-blockade gives such fast symptom relief even though it does nothing to hormone levels. In Graves disease, a stimulating autoantibody (TRAb/TSI) binds the TSH receptor and drives the whole factory continuously, uncoupled from pituitary feedback.

Think of the thyroid as a furnace with a broken thermostat. TPO is the burner assembling fuel (thionamides shut the burner off); stored hormone is fuel already in the tank (iodine slams the tank valve); deiodinase is the igniter converting fuel to flame (PTU, propranolol, steroids dampen it); and β-receptors are the air intake feeding the fire (β-blockers choke the intake). Thyroid storm is when the furnace's safety limits fail entirely and the house starts to overheat.

Every therapy in this guide maps to one arrow in the diagram: thionamides (methimazole, PTU) block TPO organification; iodine (SSKI/Lugol) blocks stored-hormone release via the acute Wolff–Chaikoff effect; high-dose PTU, propranolol, and glucocorticoids block peripheral T4→T3 conversion; β-blockers block the amplified adrenergic signal; cholestyramine traps hormone in the gut to interrupt enterohepatic recycling.

🗂️

Classification — get the vocabulary right

Thyrotoxicosis = excess thyroid hormone action (from any source). Hyperthyroidism = thyrotoxicosis specifically from overproduction by the gland. Thyroid storm = decompensated, organ-threatening thyrotoxicosis (a clinical diagnosis, not a lab value).

A low or absent radioiodine uptake in a thyrotoxic patient means the gland is not overproducing — think thyroiditis, exogenous hormone, iodine load, or struma ovarii. Thionamides don't help those (there is no active synthesis to block); you treat with β-blockers ± steroids and time.

Presentation — frequency & why

📊

Symptoms & signs of thyrotoxicosis

Frequencies are approximate and overlap across series; color reflects band (red >70%, amber 40–70%, blue 15–40%, purple <15%). Older patients often present with apathetic hyperthyroidism — weight loss, AF, and depression without the classic hyperadrenergic look.

🩺 Clinic — diagnosis, cause-finding & definitive therapy
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Outpatient presentation & who to test

Suspect hyperthyroidism with unexplained weight loss + tachycardia, new atrial fibrillation (especially <65y or without hypertension), anxiety/tremor, heat intolerance, proximal weakness, frequent stools, or oligomenorrhea. A diffuse goiter with a bruit + orbitopathy is Graves until proven otherwise.

Apathetic hyperthyroidism is the older-adult trap: instead of the classic hyperadrenergic look, they present with weight loss, depression/withdrawal, muscle wasting, and isolated atrial fibrillation or heart failure. Up to ~40% of hyperthyroid patients over 60 have AF, so a low TSH belongs in every new-AF and unexplained-weight-loss workup regardless of how "hyperthyroid" they appear.

Order a TSH first in anyone with new AF, unexplained weight loss, osteoporosis in a younger patient, or a suppressed pre-op TSH. A normal TSH essentially excludes primary hyperthyroidism.
Subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH, normal free T4/T3): treat when TSH is persistently <0.1 mIU/L and the patient is age ≥65, has cardiac disease/atrial fibrillation, or osteoporosis/postmenopausal — these carry higher AF, fracture, and mortality risk. For TSH 0.1–0.4 with none of those, observe and repeat in 3–6 months (many normalize, especially post-thyroiditis).

Why each lab moves (and what fools you)

LabDirectionMechanism / confounders
TSH↓↓Pituitary feedback shut off by high T4/T3. Falsely low in central hyperthyroidism, first-trimester pregnancy (hCG cross-reactivity), non-thyroidal illness, glucocorticoids, dopamine.
Free T4↑Overproduction/release. Can be normal in T3 toxicosis. Heparin falsely raises free T4 assays.
Total T3/T4↑Estrogen/pregnancy raise TBG → high total with normal free; always interpret with free hormone.
TRAb/TSI+Direct autoantibody assay for Graves; titer predicts relapse and neonatal risk in pregnancy.
RAIU↑ or ↓Recent iodinated contrast or amiodarone floods the gland and falsely lowers uptake for weeks.
Alk phos / Ca↑Bone turnover from thyroid hormone; mild hypercalcemia possible.

Chronic management

💊

Stepwise therapy — symptom control → antithyroid drug → definitive

1
Symptom control — β-blocker
Immediate relief while definitive therapy takes effect
▾
Blocks the amplified β-adrenergic signal — controls tachycardia, tremor, anxiety within hours. High-dose propranolol also modestly blocks peripheral T4→T3.
DrugStartTitration → targetWhy it worksIf contraindicated / alt
Propranolol10–40 mg PO q6–8h↑ q4–7 d to sx control; typically 80–160 mg/day (up to 320)Non-selective β-block + ↓T4→T3 at high dosePreferred agent in storm
Atenolol / metoprololAtenolol 25–50 mg daily; metoprolol 25–50 mg BID↑ to 100 mg/day (atenolol) as neededβ1-selective; once-daily aids adherencePreferred if mild reactive airway
Esmolol (IV)—see ICU storm protocolTitratable, ultra-short-acting for unstable patientsICU use
Diltiazem / verapamilDiltiazem 30 mg q6h → titrateRate control to HR <100Non-DHP CCB slows AV nodeAlternative when β-blocker truly contraindicated (severe asthma)
Use β-blockers cautiously in decompensated heart failure, but do not withhold in storm — uncontrolled tachycardia is often the problem. Titrate carefully, favor esmolol so it can be stopped fast.
2
Antithyroid drug (thionamide)
Methimazole is first-line for most; PTU in specific settings
▾
Thionamides inhibit TPO, halting organification and coupling → less new hormone. PTU additionally blocks peripheral D1 deiodinase (T4→T3), the reason it is favored in storm despite worse hepatotoxicity.
DrugStart (by severity)Titration → maintenanceWhy / whenKey toxicity & alt
Methimazole (MMI)FT4 1–1.5× ULN: 5–10 mg daily · 1.5–2×: 10–20 mg · 2–3×: 30–40 mg dailyRecheck FT4 q4–6 wk; step down ~50% as euthyroid; maintenance 5–10 mg dailyFirst-line: once-daily, less hepatotoxic, faster euthyroidAvoid 1st-trimester pregnancy (aplasia cutis, embryopathy). Rash → antihistamine + continue vs switch
PTU50–150 mg PO q8h (150–450 mg/day)Titrate to FT4; maintenance 50 mg BID–TIDFirst-trimester pregnancy, thyroid storm, MMI intoleranceBlack-box hepatotoxicity (FDA 2010); reserve otherwise
CarbimazolePro-drug of MMI (10 mg carbimazole ≈ 6 mg MMI)As MMIEquivalent where available (non-US)Same profile as MMI
Agranulocytosis (~0.2–0.5%, usually first 90 d): fever + sore throat → stop the drug, check CBC now. Counsel every patient. Do not switch to the other thionamide (cross-reactive) — move to RAI or surgery. Also warn of ANCA-vasculitis (PTU) and cholestatic injury (MMI).
Titrate vs block-replace: most use dose-titration monotherapy (fewer side effects). Block-replace (fixed high thionamide + levothyroxine add-back) is reserved for difficult control; it does not improve remission and raises drug exposure.
3
Definitive therapy — RAI or surgery
For Graves relapse, TMNG, toxic adenoma, or patient preference
▾

Radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation: outpatient, definitive; expect hypothyroidism (the goal) → lifelong levothyroxine. Pre-treat high-risk/cardiac patients with a thionamide to deplete stores (stop MMI ~3–5 d before to allow uptake). Contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation, and can worsen active moderate–severe Graves orbitopathy (pre-treat with glucocorticoids or choose surgery; counsel smokers to quit).

Thyroidectomy: for large compressive goiter, coexisting suspicious nodule, moderate-severe orbitopathy, pregnancy with thionamide intolerance, or need for rapid definitive cure. Render euthyroid pre-op (thionamide) and give potassium iodide (SSKI) 5–7 days pre-op to reduce gland vascularity. Risks: recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, hypoparathyroidism.

Antithyroid drugRadioiodineSurgery
Best forMild, high remission chance, pregnancyTMNG/adenoma, comorbid, wants to avoid surgeryCompression, nodule, severe orbitopathy, pregnancy + intolerance
Time to controlWeeks6–18 wkImmediate (once euthyroid)
Hypothyroid riskLow (on Rx)High (expected)High/definite

Titration & follow-up

📈

What to recheck, and when

TestCadenceWhy
Free T4 (± T3)Every 4–6 wk after start/change, then q2–3 mo once stableTSH stays suppressed for weeks — titrate to free T4/T3, not TSH early on

A Graves course of 12–18 months of thionamide gives ~30–50% durable remission; low TRAb, small goiter, and mild disease predict success. Persistent high TRAb → plan definitive therapy.
Prevent

USPSTF & special populations

🛡️

Screening evidence & pregnancy

GradeRecommendationPopulation
IScreening for thyroid dysfunction — insufficient evidence in asymptomatic non-pregnant adults (2015). Test based on symptoms/risk, not universal screening.Asymptomatic adults
—ATA/Endocrine Society: case-finding in high-risk (prior thyroid disease, AF, autoimmune disease, first-degree family history, amiodarone/lithium, neck irradiation).High-risk adults

Pregnancy — a special case

  • PTU in the first trimester (MMI embryopathy risk), then many switch to MMI in 2nd/3rd trimester to reduce PTU hepatotoxicity.
  • Target free T4 at the upper-normal range using the lowest thionamide dose; RAI is contraindicated.
  • Check TRAb in late 2nd trimester — high titers cross the placenta and can cause neonatal Graves.
  • Distinguish from gestational transient thyrotoxicosis (hCG-mediated, resolves by ~14–18 wk, no TRAb) — usually needs no thionamide.
Do not confuse Graves with gestational thyrotoxicosis — treating the latter with thionamides risks fetal hypothyroidism.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Fever + tachycardia + altered mentation or agitation, new/uncontrolled AF with rapid rate or heart failure, chest pain, temperature >38.5 °C with a known thyrotoxic state, or vomiting/jaundice — these suggest impending or established thyroid storm. Compute a Burch-Wartofsky score and go to the ED.
On a thionamide with fever or sore throat — assume agranulocytosis until CBC clears it: stop drug, urgent CBC.
🛏️ Wards — severe thyrotoxicosis, acute inpatient control
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria

  • Severe symptomatic thyrotoxicosis not controllable outpatient (HR persistently >120, weight loss with dehydration, marked agitation).
  • New rapid atrial fibrillation or high-output heart failure attributable to thyrotoxicosis.
  • Burch-Wartofsky 25–44 (impending storm) — admit for IV therapy and monitoring.
  • Agranulocytosis/neutropenic fever on a thionamide.
  • Thyrotoxicosis with a precipitant (infection, DKA, MI, surgery) needing inpatient treatment.
Any Burch-Wartofsky ≥45, hemodynamic instability, or altered mental status → treat as thyroid storm in the ICU (see ICU tab), not the floor.

Treat

Acute management

💊

Inpatient control ladder

1
β-blockade for rate/symptoms
▾

Propranolol 20–40 mg PO q6h (titrate to HR <90–100) or metoprolol; esmolol drip if unstable. In thyrotoxic AF, β-blockade is both rate control and symptom control. Anticoagulation decision per CHA₂DS₂-VASc (thyrotoxicosis alone is not an automatic indication once euthyroid).

2
Thionamide to stop synthesis
▾

Methimazole 20–40 mg/day (divided or once daily) for severe non-storm thyrotoxicosis; PTU if pregnant/first trimester or progressing toward storm. Give before any iodine.

3
Escalate to full storm protocol
▾

If Burch-Wartofsky climbs to ≥45 or organ dysfunction appears, add iodine (≥1 h after thionamide) + glucocorticoid and move to ICU (see ICU tab).

Rapid atrial fibrillation — a common thyrotoxic complication and admission trigger.

Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • HR, temperature, mental status, Burch-Wartofsky trend — the clinical response, not the lab, guides escalation.
  • Volume status & electrolytes (insensible losses from fever/sweating; replete Mg/K, glucose).
  • Telemetry for AF/rate; assess for heart failure signs.
  • Free T4/T3 every 2–3 days initially to confirm falling trend.
  • LFTs/CBC if on high-dose PTU or symptomatic.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for any of: Burch-Wartofsky ≥45; temperature >39–40 °C; altered mental status/agitation/seizure; hemodynamic instability or shock; rapid AF with heart failure/pulmonary edema; need for IV esmolol titration or invasive monitoring; refractory hyperthermia.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: HR controlled (<100 at rest), afebrile, tolerating PO, on a stable thionamide + β-blocker regimen, precipitant treated, arranged endocrine follow-up with a definitive-therapy plan, and agranulocytosis counseling given.

Home

Rate-controlled, oral regimen, reliable follow-up in 1–2 wk.

Home health

Needs INR/lab draws or teaching but otherwise stable.

SNF

Deconditioned elderly with apathetic thyrotoxicosis needing skilled care.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-storm with critical-illness myopathy tolerating ≥3h therapy/day.

LTAC

Prolonged vent weaning after storm-related respiratory failure.

Hospice / palliative

Rare — refractory storm with irreversible multi-organ failure and goals-of-care shift.
🫀 ICU — thyroid storm, the endocrine emergency
Admit

ICU triggers & scoring

🚨

Recognize thyroid storm

Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis — hormone levels are not higher than in uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis. The signature is failure of compensation: hyperpyrexia (often >39–40 °C), tachyarrhythmia out of proportion to fever, CNS dysfunction (agitation → delirium → seizure/coma), GI-hepatic failure (vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice), and cardiovascular collapse. There is almost always a precipitant: infection, surgery, trauma, DKA, MI, parturition, iodinated contrast, or abrupt thionamide withdrawal.

Do not wait for labs to confirm. If the picture fits and Burch-Wartofsky ≥45, start the full protocol immediately — mortality is ~8–25% and rises with delay.

Japan Thyroid Association (JTA/JES 2016) criteria — the more specific framework

Prerequisite for both tiers: thyrotoxicosis with elevated free T3 and/or free T4. Features: CNS (restlessness, delirium, psychosis, somnolence/coma), fever ≥38 °C, tachycardia ≥130 bpm, CHF (pulmonary edema / Killip ≥III / NYHA IV), GI–hepatic (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or total bilirubin >3.0 mg/dL).

  • TS1 (definite): thyrotoxicosis + [≥1 CNS feature AND ≥1 other feature] OR [≥3 features without CNS].
  • TS2 (suspected): thyrotoxicosis + exactly 2 features, or a TS1 combination but free T3/T4 not yet available.
Use Burch-Wartofsky to trigger urgent treatment (sensitive; good rule-out at <25) and the JTA criteria to confirm/classify (more specific; requires CNS involvement or ≥3 systems for "definite"). JTA nationwide-survey mortality was ~11% (TS1) and ~9.5% (TS2).

Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous telemetry + core temperature; arterial line if titrating esmolol or unstable.
  • Central access for concurrent infusions (esmolol, fluids, vasopressors if shock).
  • Trend: HR, temperature, mental status, urine output, glucose, Mg/K/Phos, LFTs, lactate.
  • Aggressive volume resuscitation (insensible losses can reach several liters/day); dextrose-containing fluids replenish depleted glycogen; thiamine if malnourished.
Support

Thyroid storm protocol — the order matters

💉

Four drugs, sequenced by mechanism

Sequenced storm therapy. Iodine must follow the thionamide by ≥1 h to avoid fueling synthesis (Jod-Basedow).
Step / DrugLoading → doseTitration / targetWhy it worksCautions / alt
1. Propranolol60–80 mg PO q4–6h; or 0.5–1 mg IV slow, then 1–3 mg IV q several h under monitoringHR <90–100; adrenergic symptom controlβ-blockade of amplified adrenergic drive; high dose ↓T4→T3Esmolol 250–500 mcg/kg IV load then 50–100 mcg/kg/min if unstable/CHF (titratable, stoppable)
2. PTU (thionamide FIRST)500–1000 mg PO/NG load, then 250 mg q4hContinue until improved, then convert to MMIBlocks TPO synthesis and peripheral T4→T3 — preferred in stormMethimazole 20 mg q4–6h (60–80 mg/day) if PTU unavailable/intolerant
3. Iodine (≥1 h AFTER thionamide)SSKI 5 drops (~250 mg) PO q6h; or Lugol's 8–10 drops q6–8h; or sodium iodide IVContinue 5–7 daysAcute Wolff–Chaikoff: blocks stored-hormone release & organificationLithium 300 mg q6–8h (target 0.6–1.0 mEq/L) if iodine-allergic
4. Hydrocortisone100 mg IV q8h (± 300 mg load)Taper as patient improvesBlocks T4→T3, treats relative adrenal insufficiency & possible autoimmune adrenalitisDexamethasone 2 mg IV q6h (also blocks conversion)
SupportiveAcetaminophen + cooling blankets; IV fluids; treat precipitantCore temp down; euvolemiaReduce hyperthermia & metabolic demandAvoid aspirin (displaces T4 from TBG → ↑free hormone); avoid salicylates
RefractoryCholestyramine 4 g PO QID; therapeutic plasma exchange; emergent thyroidectomyWhen not improving in 24–48 hInterrupt enterohepatic recycling; physically remove circulating hormonePlasmapheresis as bridge to surgery
This is the whole mechanism map made concrete: choke the intake (β-blocker), shut the burner (thionamide), slam the tank valve (iodine), dampen the igniter (steroid + PTU), and if still burning, bail out the fuel (cholestyramine / plasma exchange / thyroidectomy).
Sequence rule: give the thionamide first and wait ≥1 hour before iodine. Iodine in an unblocked gland provides fresh substrate and can worsen hormone synthesis (Jod-Basedow). Never give iodinated contrast to diagnose the cause during a storm.
Support

Hemodynamic support

💧

Shock in storm — mixed picture

Cardiovascular collapse in storm is complex: high-output failure, tachyarrhythmia-mediated cardiomyopathy, or distributive shock from the hypermetabolic state. Restore volume first, control rate, and support pressure as needed.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 > β10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line for distributive/mixed shock
Esmolol (for rate, not pressor)β1 antagonist250–500 mcg/kg load → 50–200 mcg/kg/min↓HR, ↓myocardial O₂ demandRate-related decompensation; titratable
Vasopressin (adjunct)V10.03 units/min fixed↑SVR, catecholamine-sparingAdd-on refractory vasodilatory shock
β-blockade in decompensated high-output failure is a tightrope — start esmolol so it can be stopped in seconds if cardiac output is rate-dependent. Digoxin (higher doses often needed) can help rate-control thyrotoxic AF with heart failure.
Airway

Respiratory support

🌬️

When intubation is needed

Most storm patients do not need mechanical ventilation for the thyroid disease itself; intubate for airway protection (obtundation/coma), agitation requiring deep sedation, or respiratory failure from pulmonary edema/high-output heart failure. There is no lung-specific pathology — use standard lung-protective settings.

Minute ventilation
High demand
hypermetabolism → high CO₂ production; watch for high RR needs
FiO₂ / PEEP
Titrate
SpO₂ 92–96%, PEEP 5–8
Thyrotoxic patients have markedly increased CO₂ production; do not under-ventilate. Avoid drugs that worsen tachyarrhythmia; ketamine's sympathomimetic effect is relatively contraindicated for induction.
Rescue

Advanced / refractory therapies

⚙️

When first-line fails

  • Cholestyramine 4 g PO QID — binds hormone in the gut, interrupts enterohepatic recirculation; adjunct that speeds T4/T3 fall.
  • Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE / plasmapheresis) — physically removes circulating hormone and antibody; use for refractory storm or as a bridge to urgent thyroidectomy.
  • Emergent thyroidectomy — definitive when medical therapy fails, thionamide is contraindicated (agranulocytosis), or amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is refractory; requires an experienced surgeon and pre-op stabilization.
  • Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT): distinguish the two types — the treatment is different (table below). Continuation vs stopping amiodarone is a joint cardiology-endocrine decision; mixed/indeterminate forms are common and often need combined therapy.
Type 1 (iodine-induced hyperthyroidism)Type 2 (destructive thyroiditis)
Underlying glandAbnormal (nodular / latent Graves)Normal
MechanismIodine load → ↑synthesis (Jod-Basedow)Drug-induced follicular destruction, hormone leak
Color Doppler flowIncreased vascularityAbsent vascularity
TreatmentMethimazole (high dose) ± potassium perchlorateGlucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone); thionamides ineffective
AmiodaroneUsually stop (cardiology input)May sometimes continue
Refractory / unstable cardiacCombine thionamide + perchlorate + steroid; total thyroidectomy for medically refractory disease
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: afebrile, HR <100 off IV agents (on oral β-blocker), mental status back to baseline, hemodynamically stable off pressors, tolerating oral thionamide + iodine, precipitant controlled, and Burch-Wartofsky trending <25. Transition IV esmolol → oral propranolol and confirm stability for 12–24 h first.
Not yet if: still febrile, requiring IV rate control, altered mentation, ongoing arrhythmia with instability, or free T4/T3 not yet trending down. A falsely reassuring HR on high-dose β-blocker can mask persistent thyrotoxicosis — recheck the whole picture.
Interactions

Comorbidity interactions & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidities change course & management

ComorbidityEffect on diseaseEffect on management
Atrial fibrillationCommon (esp. age >60); ↑stroke & heart-failure risk; poor rate control until euthyroidβ-blocker first; anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; rhythm often reverts once euthyroid (delay cardioversion until then)
Heart failure / high-outputTachyarrhythmia-mediated cardiomyopathy; decompensation in stormCautious esmolol (stoppable); diurese pulmonary edema; digoxin adjunct; treat thyrotoxicosis aggressively
PregnancyUntreated → miscarriage, pre-eclampsia, fetal loss; storm risk peripartumPTU 1st trimester → MMI later; lowest dose to keep FT4 upper-normal; no RAI; monitor TRAb for neonatal Graves
Diabetes / DKAThyrotoxicosis worsens hyperglycemia; DKA is a classic storm precipitantTreat both simultaneously; higher insulin needs during hypermetabolism
Amiodarone useType 1 (iodine load) vs Type 2 (destructive) thyrotoxicosisType 1 → thionamide ± perchlorate; Type 2 → steroids; distinguish with Doppler flow & clinical course
Adrenal insufficiencyRelative AI unmasked by hypermetabolic stressEmpiric hydrocortisone in storm covers this and blocks T4→T3
Liver diseaseBaseline transaminitis complicates thionamide monitoringFavor MMI (less hepatotoxic than PTU); trend LFTs
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: Aspirin & salicylates (displace T4 from TBG, raising free hormone — use acetaminophen for fever); iodinated contrast and amiodarone (iodine load → Jod-Basedow, can precipitate thyrotoxicosis/storm); pseudoephedrine and other sympathomimetics (add adrenergic fuel); abrupt thionamide withdrawal (classic storm trigger); giving iodine before a thionamide in an unblocked gland.
Pearls

High-yield pearls

💡

Fifteen things that change management

  1. Storm is clinical, not biochemical. Free T4/T3 in storm are no higher than in uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis — treat the syndrome and the Burch-Wartofsky score, not a number on the panel.
  2. BWPS ≥45 = treat now; 25–44 is impending storm with a low threshold to escalate. Start the bundle before confirmatory labs return.
  3. Thionamide before iodine, ≥1 h apart. Iodine given to an unblocked gland delivers fresh substrate and can worsen synthesis (Jod-Basedow). Shut down TPO first.
  4. Never aspirin in storm. Salicylates displace T4/T3 from thyroid-binding globulin, raising free hormone. Use acetaminophen and cooling instead.
  5. PTU is the storm / first-trimester thionamide (adds a peripheral T4→T3 block), but methimazole is first-line everywhere else because of PTU's hepatotoxicity boxed warning.
  6. β-blockers can kill in low-EF thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy. When output is rate-dependent, abrupt β-blockade can cause cardiogenic collapse — use titratable esmolol and get an echo.
  7. Agranulocytosis is symptom-driven. Any fever or sore throat on a thionamide → stop the drug and get an urgent CBC; routine serial CBC does not reliably catch it.
  8. A major thionamide reaction means don't cross over to the other thionamide (cross-reactive) — go to radioiodine or surgery.
  9. RAIU is contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation — diagnose Graves with TRAb + Doppler ultrasound instead.
  10. In amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis, Doppler decides therapy: increased flow (type 1) → thionamide ± perchlorate; absent flow (type 2) → glucocorticoids.
  11. Radioiodine can worsen active moderate–severe Graves orbitopathy, especially in smokers — steroid-cover or choose surgery.
  12. Follow free T4/T3, not TSH, early. TSH stays suppressed for weeks-to-months after control and will mislead you if you titrate to it.
  13. Titration beats block-replace — same remission rate, fewer adverse effects and less drug exposure.
  14. Iodinated contrast and amiodarone can precipitate thyrotoxicosis (Jod-Basedow) in nodular glands — screen before, watch after.
  15. Steroids do double duty in storm — block peripheral T4→T3 and cover the relative adrenal insufficiency of the hypermetabolic state.
For agitation in storm, olanzapine is preferred; avoid haloperidol (case reports of precipitating/worsening storm). Add VTE prophylaxis, correct electrolytes, and give dextrose-containing fluids to replete depleted glycogen.
